claim: Life-long lack of growth hormone (GH) action can produce remarkable extension of longevity in mice.
source: Life-long lack of growth hormone (GH) action can produce remarkable extension of longevity in mice.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact about GH-deficient mice.

claim: GH treatment limited to a few weeks during development influences the lifespan of long-lived Ames dwarf and normal littermate control mice in a genotype and sex-specific manner.
source: Here we report that GH treatment limited to a few weeks during development influences the lifespan of long-lived Ames dwarf and normal littermate control mice in a genotype and sex-specific manner.
evidence: This is the main finding reported in the abstract, supported by the survival data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Short period of GH exposure during early development produces persistent phenotypic, metabolic and molecular changes that are evident in late adult life.
source: Studies in a separate cohort of Ames dwarf mice show that this short period of the GH exposure during early development produces persistent phenotypic, metabolic and molecular changes that are evident in late adult life.
evidence: This claim is supported by the metabolic profiling and molecular analyses presented in Figures 4-8.

claim: Low birth weight infants born to undernourished mothers have increased risk for hypertension, cardiovascular disease and diabetes in later life.
source: Low birth weight infants born to undernourished mothers were found to have increased risk for hypertension, cardiovascular disease and diabetes in later life (Huxley et al., 2002; Xiao et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous epidemiological studies.

claim: Maternal over-nutrition and obesity are strongly associated with adult metabolic dysfunction in the offspring.
source: Furthermore, recent studies have shown that maternal over-nutrition and obesity are also strongly associated with adult metabolic dysfunction in the offspring (Curhan et al., 1996; Levin and Govek, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Moderate reduction of food or protein intake during pregnancy of female rats and mice lead to improved metabolic status and extended longevity of offspring.
source: Moderate reduction of food or protein intake during pregnancy of female rats and mice lead to improved metabolic status and extended longevity of offspring (Hales et al., 1996; Jennings et al., 1999; Ozanne and Hales, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous animal studies.

claim: A modest reduction of nutrient availability during the pre-weaning period produced by increasing the number of pups in a litter increased longevity of UM-HET3 mice.
source: We have shown that a modest reduction of nutrient availability during the pre-weaning period produced by increasing the number of pups in a litter increased longevity of UM-HET3 mice (Sun et al., 2009a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: Hormonal signals are among key determinants of mammalian longevity.
source: There is considerable evidence that hormonal signals are among key determinants of mammalian longevity, and the role of the somatotropic axis (GH-IGF-I axis) in the control of aging is particularly well documented (Bartke et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: Mice lacking GH exhibit robust and reproducible extension of both female and male longevity.
source: Robust and reproducible extension of both female and male longevity characterizes mice lacking GH (Brown-Borg et al., 1996; Flurkey et al., 2001), GH receptors (Coschigano et al., 2003) or GH-releasing hormone, the key stimulator of GH release (Sun et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Longevity is extended in mice with reduced tissue levels of bioavailable IGF-1.
source: Longevity is also extended in mice with reduced tissue levels of bioavailable IGF-1 (Conover and Bale, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The somatotropic axis influences longevity in other mammalian species including humans.
source: Importantly, there is increasing evidence that the somatotropic axis similarly influences longevity in other mammalian species including humans (Guevara-Aguirre et al., 2011; Milman et al., 2016; van der Spoel et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies in humans.

claim: GH treatment during early postnatal period had negative effect on the lifespan of male Ames dwarf mice.
source: Panici et al. reported that GH (but not thyroxine) treatment during early postnatal period had negative effect on the lifespan of male Ames dwarf mice (Panici et al., 2010) implying that the actions of GH during development can alter the trajectory of aging and that regulation of longevity may be difficult to uncouple from growth and adult body size.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study by Panici et al.

claim: Early-life GH replacement had no effect on longevity in Snell dwarf mice despite dramatic effects on growth and development.
source: In contrast, an earlier study showed that early-life GH replacement had no effect on longevity in Snell dwarf mice despite dramatic effects on growth and development (Vergara et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study by Vergara et al.

claim: Snell dwarf mice share the same endocrine defects with Ames dwarf mice and also live much longer than their normal siblings.
source: Notably, Snell dwarf mice share the same endocrine defects with Ames dwarf mice and also live much longer than their normal siblings (Flurkey et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: GH therapy during development extended longevity in dwarf rats.
source: Interestingly, in an earlier study using the dwarf rats, GH therapy during development was shown to extend longevity (Sonntag et al., 2005), but the interpretation of these findings was complicated by the unexpectedly normal lifespan of these mutants.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study in rats.

claim: Saline treated dwarf mice had dramatically extended lifespan relative to normal control mice.
source: Consistent with the previous reports (Bartke et al., 2001; Brown-Borg et al., 1996), saline treated dwarf mice had dramatically extended lifespan relative to N control mice (p<0.0001; log-rank test, both sexes).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of survival data and citations to previous reports.

claim: The median lifespan of GH treated dwarf mice (sexes combined) was decreased by 165 days (or 16%) relative to that of saline-injected dwarf mice when GH treatment was administered between the postnatal first and seventh week.
source: Being subjected to the GH treatment between the postnatal first and seventh week, the median lifespan of GH treated dwarf mice (sexes combined) was decreased by 165 days (or 16%) relative to that of saline-injected dwarf mice (839 days for GH-dwarf mice vs. 1004 days for saline-dwarf mice) (Figure 1A; left panel), (p=0.0382) based upon log-rank test.
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 1A and statistical analysis.

claim: There was no statistically significant effect of GH treatment between weeks 1-7 on the lifespan of control mice.
source: Intriguingly, there was no statistically significant (log-rank test) effect of the same GH treatment regimen on the lifespan of control mice.
evidence: This claim is based on statistical analysis of survival data.

claim: Median lifespan in male Prop1df/df mice was shortened by 204 days (20%; from 1011 to 807 days) by GH treatment between postnatal first and seventh week.
source: Analysis of each sex separately showed that median lifespan in male Prop1df/df mice was shortened by 204 days (20%; from 1011 to 807 days) by GH treatment between postnatal first and seventh week (Figure 1B,C), with the overall survival being significantly decreased (p=0.008).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 1B,C and statistical analysis.

claim: There was no significant treatment effect on overall or median survival in female dwarf mice treated with GH between weeks 1-7, indicating sex dimorphism in response to the early GH exposure.
source: There was no significant treatment effect on overall or median survival in female dwarf mice, indicating sex dimorphism in response to the early GH exposure.
evidence: This claim is based on statistical analysis of survival data in female mice.

claim: GH treatment between weeks 1-7 in dwarf mice led to a significant decrease in maximum lifespan.
source: As shown in the Figure 1A, this (weeks 1–7) protocol in dwarf mice led to a significant decrease in maximum lifespan (p=0.0462 for 25th percentile and p=0.0400 for 10th percentile) relative to vehicle controls.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantile regression analysis of survival data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The median lifespan of GH-treated dwarf mice (sexes combined) was decreased by 199 days (19.5%; from 1019 to 821 days) relative to that of vehicle-treated dwarf mice when GH was administered between postnatal second and eighth week.
source: In the setting of the second of the employed treatment protocols (GH or vehicle between postnatal second and eighth week), the median lifespan of the GH-treated dwarf mice (sexes combined) was decreased by 199 days (19.5%; from 1019 to 821 days) relative to that of vehicle-treated dwarf mice (log-rank test, p<0.0229).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data and statistical analysis.

claim: In dwarf mice treated with GH between weeks 2-8, the median lifespan was decreased by 22% in males and 19.6% in females.
source: In dwarf mice, the median lifespan was decreased by 22% (p=0.011) in males and 19.6% (p=0.048) in females.
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data and statistical analysis.

claim: GH treatment between weeks 2 and 8 significantly shortened the longevity of littermate control mice.
source: In contrast with the results of treatment earlier in life (weeks 1–7), GH treatment between weeks 2 and 8 significantly shortened the longevity of littermate control mice (log-rank test, p=0.0002), with the median lifespan reduced by 12.6%.
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data and statistical analysis.

claim: Littermate male GH-treated mice had a 19.6% decrease in mean lifespan relative to the saline group when treated between weeks 2-8.
source: Littermate male GH-treated mice had a 19.6% decrease in mean lifespan relative to the saline group (Figure 2) (log-rank test, p<0.0001) (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 2 and statistical analysis.

claim: The longevity of GH-treated littermate female mice seemed slightly decreased compared to the saline group, but this apparent difference was not statistically significant.
source: The longevity of GH-treated littermate female mice seemed slightly decreased compared to the saline group, but this apparent difference was not statistically significant (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is based on statistical analysis of survival data shown in Figure 2.

claim: GH treated dwarf mice had aging rates that increased at younger ages to a lower level relative to saline-treated dwarf mice in the first week GH treatment protocol.
source: In the first week GH treatment protocol (between postnatal first and seventh week), GH treated dwarf mice had aging rates that increased at younger ages to a lower level relative to saline-treated dwarf mice (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by aging rate analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: There was no clear effect on aging rates of normal control mice using the first week GH treatment regime.
source: There was no clear effect on aging rates of normal control mice using the same GH treatment regime.
evidence: This claim is based on aging rate analysis.

claim: In the second week of the GH protocol, GH treated dwarf mice had aging rates that increased at younger ages relative to saline controls.
source: In the second week of the GH protocol (between postnatal second and eighth week), a similar pattern was observed in GH treated dwarf mice with increased aging rates at younger ages relative to saline controls (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by aging rate analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: GH treated control mice had aging rates that increased at younger ages but did not reach the same level as the saline treated mice in later life in the second week protocol.
source: In contrast with first week results, GH treated control mice had aging rates that increased at younger ages but did not reach the same level as the saline treated mice in later life.
evidence: This claim is based on aging rate analysis.

claim: Early-life GH treatment led to a significant somatic growth of dwarf mice in comparison to the saline-treated dwarf mice.
source: As expected, early-life GH treatment led to a significant somatic growth of dwarf mice in comparison to the saline-treated dwarf mice (p<0.01; Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by body weight data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: The increase in body weight from early-life GH treatment persisted after the treatment was stopped although the growth almost leveled off.
source: This increase in body weight persisted after the treatment was stopped although the growth almost leveled off, as expected.
evidence: This claim is based on body weight data over time.

claim: Significant increase in body length was observed in GH-treated dwarf mice indicating that the body weight gain was associated with skeletal growth.
source: Notably, significant increase in body length was also observed in GH-treated dwarf mice indicating that the body weight gain was associated with skeletal growth (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by tail length measurements shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Absolute heart, kidney and liver weight were increased in GH-treated dwarf mice compared to the vehicle-injected group.
source: Moreover, absolute heart, kidney and liver weight were increased in GH-treated dwarf mice compared to the vehicle-injected group (Figure 4C; p<0.05) whereas brain weight was not affected (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by organ weight measurements shown in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: Brain weight was not affected by early-life GH treatment in dwarf mice.
source: Moreover, absolute heart, kidney and liver weight were increased in GH-treated dwarf mice compared to the vehicle-injected group (Figure 4C; p<0.05) whereas brain weight was not affected (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by brain weight measurements shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The weight of the subcutaneous white adipose tissue (WAT) was dramatically decreased by the GH treatment in dwarf mice.
source: In contrast, the weight of the subcutaneous white adipose tissue (WAT) was dramatically decreased by the GH treatment in dwarf mice (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by WAT weight measurements shown in Figure 4C.

claim: O2 consumption rate (VO2), which declines during normal aging, was found increased in the adult dwarf mice when compared with age-matched littermate control mice.
source: Similar to our previous reports (Westbrook et al., 2009), O2 consumption rate (VO2), which declines during normal aging, was found increased in the adult dwarf mice when compared with age-matched littermate control mice (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by indirect calorimetry data shown in Figure 4E and citation to previous work.

claim: The upregulation of VO2 in 18-month-old dwarf mice was almost completely abolished by the transient early GH exposure.
source: Remarkably, this upregulation of VO2 in 18-month-old dwarf mice was almost completely abolished by the transient early GH exposure (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by indirect calorimetry data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The dwarf mice had a lower RQ value than control mice.
source: The dwarf mice were found to have a lower RQ value than control mice confirming our previous observations (Westbrook et al., 2009) while early-life GH treatment significantly increased RQ value (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by RQ measurements shown in Figure 4F and citation to previous work.

claim: Early-life GH treatment significantly increased RQ value in dwarf mice.
source: The dwarf mice were found to have a lower RQ value than control mice confirming our previous observations (Westbrook et al., 2009) while early-life GH treatment significantly increased RQ value (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by RQ measurements shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Early-life GH therapy dampens the metabolic flexibility in Ames dwarf mice by reducing their capacity of greater utilization of fat as energy source.
source: These data together suggest that early-life GH therapy dampens the metabolic flexibility in Ames dwarf mice by reducing their capacity of greater utilization of fat as energy source.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the VO2 and RQ data presented.

claim: Improved insulin sensitivity and increased metabolic homeostasis are the shared features of long-lived GH-related mutant mice.
source: Improved insulin sensitivity and increased metabolic homeostasis are the shared features of long-lived GH-related mutant mice (Bartke, 2011; Bartke et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous reviews.

claim: Fasting plasma glucose and insulin concentrations were significantly reduced in dwarf mice.
source: As expected, fasting plasma glucose and insulin concentrations were significantly reduced in dwarf mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by plasma measurements.

claim: Early-life GH exposure increased both circulating insulin and glucose to the levels measured in normal littermate controls at the ages of 20 months.
source: Importantly, the early-life GH exposure increased both circulating insulin and glucose to the levels measured in normal littermate controls at the ages of 20 months (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by plasma measurements shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The adiponectin level was higher in dwarf mice than in littermate control mice and GH treatment dramatically suppressed this upregulation.
source: Similarly, the adiponectin level, a marker of insulin sensitivity, was higher in dwarf mice than in littermate control mice and GH treatment dramatically suppressed this upregulation (p<0.01; Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by adiponectin measurements shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Similar pattern of GH effect was observed in the circulating ketone bodies and LDL levels.
source: Similar pattern was also observed in the circulating ketone bodies and LDL levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by plasma measurements.

claim: Early GH administration did not affect the plasma triglycerides levels in dwarf mice.
source: Interestingly, early GH administration did not affect the plasma triglycerides levels in dwarf mice, and there were no alterations in nonesterified fatty acids (NEFA) or cholesterol level in either genotype (p=0.51).
evidence: This claim is supported by plasma measurements.

claim: There were no alterations in nonesterified fatty acids (NEFA) or cholesterol level in either genotype from early GH treatment.
source: Interestingly, early GH administration did not affect the plasma triglycerides levels in dwarf mice, and there were no alterations in nonesterified fatty acids (NEFA) or cholesterol level in either genotype (p=0.51).
evidence: This claim is supported by plasma measurements.

claim: Both male and female early GH-treated dwarf mice displayed similar sensitivity to insulin as saline-treated groups at 6 months of age.
source: Unexpectedly, both male and female early GH-treated dwarf mice displayed similar sensitivity to insulin as saline-treated groups (Figure 5B); with the reduction of blood glucose levels in response to the insulin challenge paralleling between the two groups.
evidence: This claim is supported by insulin tolerance test data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Male GH-treated dwarf mice exhibited dampened sensitivity to insulin at 18 months of age in comparisons to the saline-treated groups.
source: As seen in Figure 5B, male GH-treated dwarf mice exhibited dampened sensitivity to insulin in comparisons to the saline-treated groups (*, p>0.05; at time points measured); whereas female GH-treated dwarf mice had similar response to that measured in the saline groups (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by insulin tolerance test data shown in Figure 5B (note: there appears to be a typo in the manuscript as p>0.05 would indicate non-significance, but the text suggests significance).

claim: Female GH-treated dwarf mice had similar insulin response to that measured in the saline groups at 18 months of age.
source: As seen in Figure 5B, male GH-treated dwarf mice exhibited dampened sensitivity to insulin in comparisons to the saline-treated groups (*, p>0.05; at time points measured); whereas female GH-treated dwarf mice had similar response to that measured in the saline groups (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by insulin tolerance test data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The stress responsive pathways including RAS-MAPK and PI3K-Akt play a critical role in lifespan extension in flies and worms.
source: Recent evidence has shown that the stress responsive pathways including RAS-MAPK and PI3K-Akt play a critical role in lifespan extension in flies and worms (Longo and Fabrizio, 2002; Slack et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies in invertebrates.

claim: Erk and Akt signaling are diminished, in response to multiple forms of stress, in cells and tissues from long-lived GH deficient mice.
source: Our previous studies have shown that Erk and Akt signaling are diminished, in response to multiple forms of stress, in cells and tissues from long-lived GH deficient mice (Sun et al., 2011, 2009b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the authors' previous work.

claim: Dwarf mice had lower hepatic phosphorylation of MAPKs, including the ERK1/2, P38 and Akt kinases.
source: In contrast to the littermate control mice, dwarf mice had lower hepatic phosphorylation of MAPKs, including the ERK1/2, P38 and Akt kinases, each of which is known to participate in cellular stress responses (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The livers of GH-treated dwarf mice had elevated levels of phosphorylated EKR1/2, P38 and Akt (ser473) which were indistinguishable from those measured in control mice.
source: However, the livers of GH-treated dwarf mice had elevated levels of phosphorylated EKR1/2, P38 and Akt (ser473) which were indistinguishable from those measured in control mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data.

claim: Akt phosphorylation on Thr308 was not altered by early GH treatment.
source: Interestingly, Akt phosphorylation on Thr308 was not altered (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Immediate early genes (IEG) including Egr-1, Fra1, Fos, and Jun are rapidly and transiently induced in response to stress or mitogen.
source: IEG including Egr-1, Fra1, Fos, and Jun are rapidly and transiently induced in response to stress or mitogen (Criswell et al., 2005; Sukhatme et al., 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Akt and MAPK signaling regulate IEG induction.
source: Importantly, Akt and MAPK signaling have been found to regulate IEG induction (Murphy et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Hepatic IEGs mRNA levels were significantly lower in saline-treated dwarf mice than in littermate control mice.
source: By qRT-PCR, hepatic IEGs mRNA levels were found to be significantly lower in saline-treated dwarf mice than in littermate control mice (Figure 6B) whereas early-life GH reversed this suppression and even augmented Egr-1 and Fra-1 mRNA levels above the values detected in control mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Early-life GH reversed the suppression of IEGs and even augmented Egr-1 and Fra-1 mRNA levels above the values detected in control mice.
source: By qRT-PCR, hepatic IEGs mRNA levels were found to be significantly lower in saline-treated dwarf mice than in littermate control mice (Figure 6B) whereas early-life GH reversed this suppression and even augmented Egr-1 and Fra-1 mRNA levels above the values detected in control mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Hepatic IGF-I mRNA levels followed a similar pattern to IEGs in response to early GH treatment.
source: Consistently, hepatic IGF-I mRNA levels, GH sensitive markers, followed a similar pattern (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: One of the hallmarks of aging is a state of chronic low-grade inflammation in multiple tissues.
source: One of the hallmarks of aging is a state of chronic low-grade inflammation in multiple tissues.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about aging.

claim: 20-month-old dwarf mice exhibited lower mRNA levels of several proinflammatory cytokines including IL-6, IL-1β, MCP-1, TNF-α and Socs3 particularly in WAT and liver.
source: As shown in Figures 7A and 20-month-old dwarf mice exhibited lower mRNA levels of several proinflammatory cytokines including IL-6, IL-1β, MCP-1, TNF-α and Socs3 particularly in WAT and liver.
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Early GH treatment of dwarf mice increased expression of the inflammatory cytokines in adipose and hepatic tissues to the level of the age-matched littermate control mice.
source: Importantly, early GH treatment of dwarf mice increased expression of the inflammatory cytokines in adipose and hepatic tissues to the level of the age-matched littermate control mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data.

claim: Brain tissues (cortex) showed no effect of early GH treatment on inflammatory cytokine expression, in contrast to other tissues.
source: Interestingly, brain tissues (cortex), in contrast to other tissues, showed no such effect.
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data.

claim: GH-treated dwarf mice exhibited elevated hepatic JNK phosphorylation.
source: Consistent with the data of inflammatory cytokines expression, GH-treated dwarf mice exhibited elevated hepatic JNK phosphorylation and even a larger increase in NF-kB activation in livers (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: GH-treated dwarf mice exhibited even a larger increase in NF-kB activation in livers.
source: Consistent with the data of inflammatory cytokines expression, GH-treated dwarf mice exhibited elevated hepatic JNK phosphorylation and even a larger increase in NF-kB activation in livers (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Both P-JNK and P-IkB levels were increased in WAT from GH injected dwarf mice.
source: Moreover, both P-JNK and P-IkB levels were also increased in WAT from GH injected dwarf mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data.

claim: The liver is a major organ to detoxify and eliminate xenobiotics and endobiotics which plays a key role in the metabolic homeostasis of the organism.
source: The liver is a major organ to detoxify and eliminate xenobiotics and endobiotics which plays a key role in the metabolic homeostasis of the organism (Österreicher and Trauner, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous review.

claim: Activation of xenobiotic signaling is linked with delayed aging and increased lifespan in GH-related mutant mice.
source: Recent studies in GH-related mutant mice have linked the activation of xenobiotic signaling with delayed aging and increased lifespan (Amador-Noguez et al., 2007; Steinbaugh et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The hepatic expression of xenobiotic genes was greatly upregulated in saline-treated dwarf as compared to the littermate control mice.
source: Consistent with the previous reports (Amador-Noguez et al., 2004), the hepatic expression of these xenobiotic genes was greatly upregulated in saline-treated dwarf as compared to the littermate control mice as shown in Figure 6A (p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data and citation to previous work.

claim: Early-life GH treatment dramatically suppressed the elevation of xenobiotic genes including Cyp2b9, Cyp2b13, Hao3, FMO3 and Sth2.
source: Early-life GH treatment dramatically suppressed the elevation of these genes including Cyp2b9, Cyp2b13, Hao3, FMO3 and Sth2 (two-tailed t-test; p<0.001) (Figure 8A).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: There was no effect of early GH treatment on Gapdh mRNA, the housekeeping control gene.
source: There was no such effect on Gpadh mRNA, the housekeeping control gene.
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data.

claim: Farnesoid X receptor (FXR) is a crucial factor in the regulation of xenobiotic detoxification genes in mice.
source: Several reports have pointed out that farnesoid X receptor (FXR) is a crucial factor in the regulation of xenobiotic detoxification genes in mice (Amador-Noguez et al., 2007; Lee et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: FXR protein level was increased in the dwarf livers despite the lack of difference in the mRNA levels of FXR between the two genotypes.
source: We found that FXR protein level was increased in the dwarf livers (Figure 8B) despite the lack of difference in the mRNA levels of FXR between the two genotypes.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Early-life GH treatment almost completely suppressed the upregulation of hepatic FXR protein in dwarf mice.
source: Interestingly, as shown in Figure 8B, early-life GH treatment almost completely suppressed the upregulation of hepatic FXR protein in dwarf mice, indicating that the regulatory impact of the FXR activity on hepatic xenobiotic genes is dependent on GH signaling pathways during early-life.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The regulatory impact of the FXR activity on hepatic xenobiotic genes is dependent on GH signaling pathways during early-life.
source: Interestingly, as shown in Figure 8B, early-life GH treatment almost completely suppressed the upregulation of hepatic FXR protein in dwarf mice, indicating that the regulatory impact of the FXR activity on hepatic xenobiotic genes is dependent on GH signaling pathways during early-life.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the FXR protein data and xenobiotic gene expression data.

claim: Reduced growth in utero followed by rapid postnatal catch-up growth shortened lifespan in rodents.
source: Earlier studies in rodents have shown that reduced growth in utero followed by rapid postnatal catch-up growth shortened lifespan (Jennings et al., 1999; Ozanne and Hales, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Offspring that were nursed by dams fed a low protein diet had increased lifespan.
source: Interestingly, Ozanne et al. also found that offspring that were nursed by dams fed a low protein diet, had increased lifespan (Ozanne and Hales, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Alterations of the nutritional status during the suckling period modified the growth trajectories and metabolic plasticity in late life through the regulations of the GHRH-GH-IGF-axis in mice.
source: Intriguingly, Holzenberger and colleagues reported that alterations of the nutritional status during the suckling period modified the growth trajectories and metabolic plasticity in late life through the regulations of the GHRH-GH-IGF-axis in mice (Kappeler et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: GH treatment from postnatal day 3 to day 22 could ameliorate or reverse the detrimental consequences of maternal under-nutrition in rats.
source: It is noteworthy that a series of studies in rats conducted by Vickers and his colleagues have shown that GH treatment from postnatal day 3 to day 22 could ameliorate or reverse the detrimental consequences of maternal under-nutrition indicating that hormonal intervention during this critical period can override prenatal predispostion (Gray et al., 2014, 2013; Li et al., 2015; Reynolds et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies in rats.

claim: Disrupting the GH signaling during adulthood by induced disruption of the GHR gene did not affect the median lifespan of the mice although it led to a modest increase in the maximal lifespan of the females.
source: A recent report has shown that disrupting the GH signaling during adulthood by induced disruption of the GHR gene did not affect the median lifespan of the mice although it led to a modest increase in the maximal lifespan of the females (Junnila et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The periods between the first and the eighth week of postnatal life represent a critical developmental time window in which longevity and aging rate could be programmed by GH signals.
source: Consistent with these evidences, our study pinpoints the periods between the first and the eighth week of postnatal life as a bona fide critical developmental time window in which longevity and aging rate could be programmed by GH signals.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing effects of GH treatment during these specific time windows.

claim: Decreased insulin and glucose levels together with improved insulin sensitivity are associated with slow-aging.
source: As indicated in multiple studies of long-lived mice with mutations affecting the somatotropic axis and mice on long-term calorie restriction, decreased insulin and glucose levels together with improved insulin sensitivity are associated with slow-aging most likely mechanistically (Bartke, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous review.

claim: Somatotropic mutant mice have markedly increased oxygen consumption (VO2) per unit of body weight and concomitantly reduced respiratory quotient (RQ).
source: Notably, these somatotropic mutant mice have markedly increased oxygen consumption (VO2) per unit of body weight and concomitantly reduced respiratory quotient (RQ) (Westbrook et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The advantageous metabolic features of long-lived mice are established during the early postnatal life and are particularly susceptible to the alterations in hormonal environments.
source: Our findings suggest that the advantageous metabolic features of these long-lived mice are established during the early postnatal life and are particularly susceptible to the alterations in hormonal environments.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing that early GH treatment reverses metabolic advantages.

claim: First few weeks of postnatal life represent a critical window in which the set points related to aging and longevity are programed by the hormonal milieu.
source: Taken together, this evidence suggests that that first few weeks of postnatal life represent a critical window in which the set points related to aging and longevity are programed by the hormonal milieu.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results.

claim: It may be difficult or perhaps impossible to completely uncouple the extended longevity of these animals from the reductions in somatic growth and adult body size.
source: Another important implications of the present findings is that it may be difficult or perhaps impossible to completely uncouple the extended longevity of these animals from the reductions in somatic growth and adult body size.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Stress responsive pathways play a critical role in delayed aging and extended longevity.
source: A number of lines of evidence suggest that stress responsive pathways play a critical role in delayed aging and extended longevity (Miller, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous review.

claim: Long-lived mutant mice are characterized by decreased hepatic phosphorylation of stress related kinases, including the ERK, P38 and Akt.
source: It is worthwhile to note that long-lived mutant mice were characterized by decreased hepatic phosphorylation of stress related kinases, including the ERK, P38 and Akt, each of which is known to participate in cellular stress responses (Hsieh and Papaconstantinou, 2006; Sun et al., 2011, 2009b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Chronic low-grade inflammation contributes to the development of age-related diseases and degenerative pathology during aging.
source: Chronic low-grade inflammation contributes to the development of age-related diseases and degenerative pathology during aging.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about aging.

claim: Activation of proinflammatory signaling pathways including JNK and NF-kB activity is an important pathophysiological mechanism in mediating the age-associated inflammatory processes.
source: Activation of proinflammatory signaling pathways including JNK and NF-kB activity has been recognized as an important pathophysiological mechanism in mediating the age-associated inflammatory processes (Cai and Liu, 2012; Hirosumi et al., 2002; Tuncman et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Activation of proinflammatory pathways including JNK and NF-kB may contribute to the loss of metabolic advantages and decrease of longevity in dwarf mice subjected to early-life GH exposure.
source: Together, these data suggest that activation of proinflammatory pathways including JNK and NF-kB may contribute to the loss of metabolic advantages and decrease of longevity in dwarf mice subjected to early-life GH exposure.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: A generalized up-regulation of many hepatic mRNAs for xenobiotic detoxification enzymes (XDE) represents a shared signature of long-lived mice and may be a general mechanism of slow-aging.
source: Previous studies by us and others suggest that a generalized up-regulation of many hepatic mRNAs for xenobiotic detoxification enzymes (XDE) represents a shared signature of long-lived mice and may be a general mechanism of slow-aging (Amador-Noguez et al., 2004; Shore and Ruvkun, 2013; Sun et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Mammals during the early development stage respond to their early-life hormonal environment and set anatomical, physiological and biochemical trajectories that shape their future life course including aging and longevity.
source: We speculate that mammals during the early development stage respond to their early-life hormonal environment and set anatomical, physiological and biochemical trajectories that shape their future life course including aging and longevity.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Normal siblings (df/+ or N) of Ames dwarf mice are heterozygous for the Prop1df mutation and phenotypically not distinguishable from wild type mice.
source: In our study, normal siblings (df/+ or N) of Ames dwarf mice were used as controls. These control mice are heterozygous for the Prop1df mutation and phenotypically not distinguishable from wild type mice.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental model used.

claim: Aging rates were calculated non-parametrically per group of mice per age interval of 200 days.
source: Aging rates were calculated non-parametrically as described previously (Koopman et al., 2016). First, mortality rates were calculated per group of mice per age interval of 200 days by dividing the number of mice that died by the number of days lived by all mice in the age interval of interest.
evidence: This describes the methodology used for aging rate calculations.

claim: The effects of transient early GH action on gene expression and consequent functional alterations in various tissues persist into mid- and late adult life and may indeed be permanent.
source: Our results suggest that the effects of the transient early GH action on gene expression and consequent functional alterations in various tissues persist into mid- and late adult life and may indeed be permanent.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that effects are still present at 18-20 months of age.

claim: Early-life GH administrations significantly increased or normalized the indices of hypothalamic inflammation in the middle-aged Ames dwarf mice.
source: In agreement with these observations, Sadagurski et al. found that early-life GH administrations significantly increased or normalized the indices of hypothalamic inflammation in the middle-aged Ames dwarf mice (Sadagurski et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Early GH signaling plays a key role in setting-up the xenobiotic regulation pattern in later life.
source: These data indicate that early GH signaling plays a key role in setting-up the xenobiotic regulation pattern in later life.
evidence: This is inferred from the xenobiotic gene expression data.

claim: GH signals during the early critical period have long-lasting effects on inflammation status in some tissues i.e. WAT and liver but not in other tissues such as cortex.
source: These data suggest that GH signals during the early critical period have long-lasting effects on inflammation status in some tissues i.e. WAT and liver but not in other tissues such as cortex.
evidence: This is inferred from the tissue-specific inflammatory gene expression data.

claim: Early transient GH exposure influences the inflammatory status in late life in sensitive tissues including WAT and liver.
source: Together, these data clearly showed that early transient GH exposure influences the inflammatory status in late life in sensitive tissues including WAT and liver.
evidence: This is inferred from the inflammatory marker data.

claim: The observation that early GH treatment can shorten the longevity of littermate control mice is novel and potentially important.
source: The observation that early GH treatment can shorten the longevity of littermate control mice is novel and potentially important.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of their findings.

claim: Increasing GH action during early post-natal life leads to a reduction of longevity even if GH signals are not altered after eight weeks of age, which is more than 90% of the animal lifespan.
source: It can be interpreted as additional evidence that GH actions during development predispose to accelerating aging. Thus, increasing GH action during early post-natal life leads to a reduction of longevity even if GH signals are not altered after eight weeks of age, which is more than 90% of the animal lifespan.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental design and results.

claim: Longevity was shortened by exogenous GH only in N male and in only one of the two experiment protocols.
source: It is noteworthy that longevity was shortened by exogenous GH only in N male and in only one of the two experiment protocols.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental results.
